primary_meaning: The pearl primarily symbolizes the Kingdom of Heaven (or the salvation/gospel found in it) as a treasure of supreme, surpassing worth — something so valuable that a person should gladly give up everything else to obtain it. By extension it stands for sacred, precious spiritual truth.
primary_basis: Matthew 13:45-46 (the Parable of the Pearl of Great Price: the kingdom of heaven likened to a merchant who sells all he has to buy one pearl of great value)
Matthew 7:6 ('do not cast your pearls before swine' — pearls as holy, precious truth not to be treated with contempt)
Revelation 21:21 (the twelve gates of the New Jerusalem each made of a single pearl, associating pearls with the glory and worth of God's kingdom)

alternatives.meaning: Christ himself as the pearl of great price — the believer surrenders everything to gain Christ (Phil 3:7-8 often cited in support).

The reversed reading: the merchant is Christ and the pearl is the Church or the individual believer, whom Christ 'purchased' at the cost of everything (his life). Popular in some evangelical and dispensational teaching.
Pearls as worldly luxury, ostentation, and moral corruption — adornment of the immodest or of 'Babylon the Great,' symbolizing wealth opposed to godliness.

Patristic/mystical readings of the pearl as the soul, purity, or the incarnate Word (e.g., the pearl formed in the oyster as an image of the virgin birth in some early Christian and Syriac writings such as Ephrem the Syrian's Hymns on the Pearl).

Gnostic-influenced reading of the pearl as the divine soul lost in the material world (as in the 'Hymn of the Pearl' from the Acts of Thomas) — sometimes referenced in scholarship but not mainstream Christian teaching.
basis: Acts of Thomas (Hymn of the Pearl, extracanonical)

notes: There is a broadly settled consensus that the pearl symbolizes something of supreme spiritual value — most commonly the Kingdom of Heaven/salvation per Matthew 13:45-46, with Matthew 7:6 supporting the sense of holy truth. The chief live interpretive debate concerns the parable's direction: whether the seeker is the believer (pearl = kingdom/Christ) or Christ (pearl = church/believer); both readings are widely taught. A distinct negative valence (pearls as luxury and worldliness) coexists in the New Testament and is recognized in standard commentaries, but it does not displace the dominant positive symbolism.
